title: Your First Write
description: Now you know the register map across the six Remote I/O modules. Time to write something. But think before you type — in the Tennessee Eastman process, every change has a physical consequence. Adjust a feed rate slightly. Watch what happens to pressure, level, and composition. Understand cause and effect before you push harder. The PLC at 192.168.95.2 is running a control loop that scans every 20ms — it will fight your changes unless you find the right way around it.
objectives: Write to a holding register on one of the Remote I/O modules and observe the effect on the plant
Understand the relationships: feed rates affect level, level affects pressure, composition shifts change reaction dynamics
Discover the PLC coil %QX0.0 (manual_mode) — understand what happens when it's set versus cleared
Push reactor pressure above normal (~2700 kPa) toward the override threshold (~2900 kPa)
Notice the PLC's control loop overwriting your changes — figure out why and how to persist your writes
learning_points: The PLC scans every 20ms — it reads Remote I/O inputs, runs Tennessee Eastman control logic, and writes outputs back
Your Modbus writes compete with the PLC's writes. Unless you outpace the scan cycle or disable automatic control, the PLC wins
The %QX0.0 coil (manual_mode) is a key attack vector — it determines whether the PLC actively controls the process or leaves outputs alone
Small changes in feed composition propagate through the reactor — the Tennessee Eastman process is intentionally unstable in open loop
In a real plant, what seems like a minor tweak can cascade into a pressure excursion or composition upset
things_to_think_about: Why did the PLC override your change? What does its 20ms scan cycle mean for an attacker?
What's the difference between changing a setpoint and directly overriding an actuator output?
How does manual_mode (%QX0.0) change the playing field for an attacker?
If you were the operator watching the HMI, would you have noticed what you just did?
Watch the 3D plant visualization at localhost:80 — can you see the physical effect of your writes?
flag_hint: The flag is the PLC coil address (IEC 61131-3 notation) that enables manual mode, the key to persistent process manipulation: FLAG{address}
blue_team_check: Check the Suricata alert log on the router for Modbus write function codes crossing the network. How many writes did you send before the process visibly changed? Would a rate-based alert have caught you?
